sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of systematic reviews of randomized trials (>= 6 weeks) in healthy adults, mostly novices; standard, circuit, elastic-band and home-based resistance training versus control and between prescriptions.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control, including elastic-band and home-based training. Strength is enhanced by >= 2 sessions/week, heavier loads, multiple sets and exercise at the start of the session and is not affected by machines versus free weights. Hypertrophy is enhanced by >= 10 sets/muscle group/week and is not affected by frequency when volume is equated. Data are insufficient for varied exercise selection, single- versus multi-joint hypertrophy, Nordic hamstring and Olympic-style lifting. Periodization and variation are less important than once thought.
sources.locator: Reused R6 source (r12 manifest); local Europe PMC XML audits/domain-coaching-r6-2026-10-26/reviews/ssctr-evidence/PMC12965823.xml, SHA-256 re-verified equal to the manifest on 2026-10-31; re-read this session: Eligibility Criteria; Results (Strength, Hypertrophy, Improving hypertrophy); Discussion (progressive overload, specificity and individualization, variation).
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
Exercise-level choices (which squat, row or calf raise) are not compared.
counterevidence: Insufficient data on varied selection and single- versus multi-joint hypertrophy; no specific configuration is shown superior.

For athletes who started in WALK_JOG or RESTART mode, the two qualifying weeks must lie in a block executed entirely in EASY mode after exit: the first block boundary after exit is not an assessing boundary when that block began in WALK_JOG or RESTART mode. For EASY_LOW starters the rule applies as written.

Qualifying weeks count only executed non-establishment EASY-mode weeks whose EASY and LONG gates were ADVANCE or EARNED (policy activationCounts); running minutes are executed continuous-running minutes from the completed-work ledger (walks and walk breaks excluded); a week with a missing, partial-only, conflicted or adverse report, or without a gating weekly review (R18), does not qualify.

Entry only at threshold ladder step 0 with EFFORT_CUE (talk test, about 6-7 of 10); the first exposure is recorded as a calibration; no pace target; progression one ladder step per executed comparable session without an adverse signal.
In the week quality is introduced no other run dimension steps (easy and long run hold), and the single-run ceiling applies to the whole session including warm-up and cool-down.

The introduction is disclosed as a new harder session with an easy-run alternative that the athlete may keep without penalty or volume debt; declining keeps the easy plan and may be revisited at the next block boundary.

A single adverse response repeats the step; two comparable adverse responses within 14 days regress one step; pain, injury, illness or a functional limitation routes CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED with no substitute dose; missing current eligibility is ASK.

conditions: Scope: only a task of the ACF-G05 VO2_STYLE category (minutes-long repeated harder aerobic bouts with recoveries) that is current by the R6 intake definition (flagged current, familiar and tolerated, observedAt within 28 days) and has every SSCTR-R2-P14 input (exact recipe identity, tolerance fact, target with method, construct and provenance, same-task dose and response history, comparable surface, grade and weather); familiar short-interval or speed, hill, time-trial or race-simulation tasks are not covered (LATER_GATE); an ambiguous category is ASK.

All R6 quality gates apply: run goal RACE or PERFORMANCE, at least 3 chosen run days, EASY mode, BUILD, DEVELOPMENT or NEXT_BLOCK only (week 1 only inside the reported weekly minutes per R6-COLD-START C7; never SPECIFIC, TAPER, race window or post-event); it is the week's single quality session and is not placed the day before or after the long run when another chosen run day can hold it.

The dose is held exactly: no added repetition, density, pace or duration; SSCTR-R2-P07 permits only fewer repetitions at the same target and recovery after repeated last-repetition degradation; otherwise fall back to the threshold ladder (new family: step 0 at effort cue, calibration) or to easy running, disclosed as a different stimulus.

The familiar target is a field-session task anchor only, never LT2, CS, MLSS, VO2max or race pace, with no transfer to another family, recipe or distance; the effort cue is co-primary; changed conditions or conflicting data invalidate target reuse (ASK or HOLD).

After a SHORT break the first quality slot runs easy; no quality in RETURN or RESTART mode; after a RESTART or any interruption the familiar status lapses until the task is current again under the intake definition.

It does not count as an executed threshold session for the RUN.EVENT_SPECIFIC prerequisite, nor as the achieved peak quality for taper doses, nor as executed comparable quality for the race-week touch.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of systematic reviews of randomized trials (>= 6 weeks) in healthy adults, mostly novices; standard, circuit, elastic-band and home-based resistance training versus control and between prescriptions.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control, including elastic-band and home-based training. Strength is enhanced by >= 2 sessions/week, heavier loads, multiple sets and exercise at the start of the session and is not affected by machines versus free weights. Hypertrophy is enhanced by >= 10 sets/muscle group/week and is not affected by frequency when volume is equated. Data are insufficient for varied exercise selection, single- versus multi-joint hypertrophy, Nordic hamstring and Olympic-style lifting. Periodization and variation are less important than once thought.

sources.title: Acute Neuromuscular, Physiological and Performance Responses After Strength Training in Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: de Carvalho e Silva GI, Brandao LHA, dos Santos Silva D, de Jesus Alves MD, Aidar FJ, et al.

sources.title: Triceps surae muscle hypertrophy is greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training.
sources.authors: Kinoshita M, Maeo S, Kobayashi Y, Eihara Y, Ono M, Sato M, Sugiyama T, Kanehisa H, Isaka T.
sources.population_design_dose: Non-randomized within-subject controlled training study (legs counterbalanced by dominance): 14 untrained adults; 12 weeks; standing (knee extended) versus seated (knee 90 degrees) calf raises; 5 x 10 at 70% 1RM twice weekly; MRI volumes.
sources.findings: Standing training produced much greater gastrocnemius (lateral 12.4% vs 1.7%; medial 9.2% vs 0.6%) and whole triceps-surae (5.6% vs 2.1%) hypertrophy than seated training; soleus hypertrophy was similar (2.1% vs 2.9%).
sources.locator: Read: Abstract, Introduction, Training program (allocation). Retrieved full-text XML SHA-256 f85c51afe4246fb4ae18343e565ad627295242796c56ebcaa4113d5a9131b489.
limitations: n = 14 untrained adults; hypertrophy only (strength not compared because of cross-education); machines; not runners.
counterevidence: Soleus force demands in running may justify knee-flexed work for reasons other than hypertrophy; not tested.

sources.title: Effects of training with elastic resistance versus conventional resistance on muscular strength: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Lopes JSS, Machado AF, Micheletti JK, de Almeida AC, Cavina AP, Pastre CM.
sources.population_design_dose: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 trials comparing elastic resistance (tubes, bands) with conventional resistance (machines, dumbbells) for strength in varied populations.
sources.findings: No difference between elastic and conventional resistance for lower-limb (SMD -0.11, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.19) or upper-limb strength (SMD 0.09, -0.18 to 0.35) per the corrected abstract; the 2020 corrigendum (PMC7485002) fixes a reporting error (-0.011 to -0.11).
sources.locator: Read: Abstract, Introduction, Discussion and limitations; corrigendum PMC7485002 read. Retrieved full-text XML SHA-256 248b470624788bf379bb723bf254ab4f9fa5f0fb87a6368aeff781da28aef8a1.
limitations: 8 heterogeneous low-quality trials; elastic load not standardized; mixed populations including clinical.
counterevidence: Standard resistance training improved multicomponent function more than elastic training in one comparison (R6-S01).

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of systematic reviews of randomized trials (>= 6 weeks) in healthy adults, mostly novices; standard, circuit, elastic-band and home-based resistance training versus control and between prescriptions.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control, including elastic-band and home-based training. Strength is enhanced by >= 2 sessions/week, heavier loads, multiple sets and exercise at the start of the session and is not affected by machines versus free weights. Hypertrophy is enhanced by >= 10 sets/muscle group/week and is not affected by frequency when volume is equated. Data are insufficient for varied exercise selection, single- versus multi-joint hypertrophy, Nordic hamstring and Olympic-style lifting. Periodization and variation are less important than once thought.

sources.title: The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains.
sources.authors: Pelland JC, Remmert JF, Robinson ZP, Hinson SR, Zourdos MC.
sources.population_design_dose: Bayesian multilevel meta-regressions of 67 studies (2058 participants) of weekly set volume and frequency.
sources.findings: Fractional set counting (indirect sets = 0.5) had the strongest relative evidence; volume increases hypertrophy and strength with diminishing returns; frequency increases strength (diminishing returns) with negligible effect on hypertrophy.
sources.locator: Abstract read on 2026-10-31.
limitations: Abstract only; mostly young men.
counterevidence: Dose-response curves are group means, not individual prescriptions.

applicability: Metadata used as ordinal priors and representation conventions for all 76 configurations; no dose, timer or score.

decision.rationale: The classifications are internally consistent ordinal priors and the representation corrections remove fabricated precision (kilograms for bands and assistance, per-hand values for single implements, an external load for the pull-up, bilateral logging for one-sided holds). Remaining risks are uses beyond ordinal priors: double counting through the derived recovery-cost class, adequacy claims from a non-validated set-counting convention, an implicit increment for single implements and superiority claims for bent-knee calf work. Conditions close these.
preserve: Ordinal-only semantics of demand classes
SINGLE_IMPLEMENT, BAND_TENSION, ASSISTED_BODYWEIGHT and bodyweight pull-up representation
Per-side logging of side plank and Pallof press
decision.mec_change_level: Metadata and representation only; no dose.
decision.trade_off: Better selection and placement information at the risk of overreading ordinal classes; conditions keep them ordinal.
must_not: No demand class used as a fatigue measurement, recovery timer, readiness score or additive load.
No kilogram value for bands or assistance.
No sets-per-muscle adequacy claim from the counting convention.
conditions: Demand classes, muscles and purposes are ordinal priors for comparing alternatives and placing sessions only, never a fatigue measurement, recovery timer, readiness or injury-risk score, and never summed.

The derived session recovery-cost class is explanatory and a tie-break only: it never adds a cost to a pair already costed by CMP.I01-CMP.I11 (no double counting, SIL-I4) and it follows the same phase and dose adjustment as the lower class, so an axial-HIGH row at a reduced phase dose does not by itself make a session HIGH.

Muscle counting is descriptive only: it may not set, gate or judge weekly volume adequacy until G02 adopts a reviewed method; evidence favouring fractional counting (indirect sets 0.5) is the re-review trigger.

SINGLE_IMPLEMENT progresses by the per-implement step policy:operational.strength.smallestIncrement.PER_HAND applied to the one implement, or by repetitions when that implement step is unavailable, never a fabricated load (B0-F07 made explicit in R7-B).

BAND_TENSION and ASSISTED_BODYWEIGHT never carry kilograms: they progress by repetitions inside the goal range; a level change is athlete-reported and confirmed (ASK), never inferred; a logged band or assistance value is never converted to a load.
Bent-knee calf configurations are labelled soleus emphasis (activation) without a hypertrophy or performance superiority claim; straight-knee remains the calf default.

The R6 runtime representation (PER_HAND single implements, band rows in kilograms, EXTERNAL pull-up, bilateral side plank and Pallof press) is not authority for these configurations; correcting it is an R7-B binding item (B0-F01, B0-F02).
Any change to a demand class, primary muscle or convention is a material change that invalidates this record for the affected configuration.

confidence.rationale: Representation corrections are clearly correct; ordinal demand classes are reasonable expert priors without exercise-level validation.

limitations: Targeted appraisal by a software reviewer, not a systematic review; no GRADE rating performed.
Sources marked ABSTRACT_ONLY support context only, never a prescriptive rule.
Validator and witness results prove specification structure, not training efficacy or safety.
Ordinal classes rest on mechanism and indirect evidence.

sources.authors: Mannarino P, Matta T, Lima J, Simão R, Freitas de Salles B.
sources.population_design_dose: 10 untrained men; within-subject; 8 weeks; one arm unilateral dumbbell row, the other biceps curl; 4-6 sets of 8-12 to failure, twice weekly.

decision.rationale: Systematic accessory variation and occasional purposeful main-lift changes at block boundaries are compatible with similar strength and hypertrophy outcomes and may support motivation, provided the essential stimulus is preserved, each new exercise is calibrated by effort and placed away from protected runs, and the stated cadences are not exceeded. The mapping is consistent with DR-134 and the OB-2 Q3 conditions.
preserve: MAIN stable within a block; PRACTICE reason-only
Rotation permitted, never mandatory
Effort-guided establishment with no load transfer
decision.mec_change_level: Selection change only; keeping the configuration is always the default.
decision.trade_off: Variety and motivation against novelty cost and a restart of lift-specific load tracking.
must_not: No random or redundant variation; no variation for its own sake in a MAIN slot.
No load transfer between configurations.
No rotation in deferred phases or during return steps.
conditions: Rotation is selection only, permitted never mandatory, systematic never random: an admissible alternative keeps the slot pattern and subpattern (or the LUNGE split-stance and step group), shares a primary muscle, stays within one step on lower, axial and eccentric class, fits equipment and skill, admits the slot role and does not worsen the week's arrangement cost.

Every newly rotated or re-introduced configuration is a calibration exposure: effort-guided establishment (at most 2 sets at RIR >= 3, ascending ramp), no load transferred, no progression step in its first exposure, earlier sets returning one per executed week (R6-ROTATION C7, C8, C10, C12); its first exposure follows B0-C11 placement away from the long run and the week's quality run.
No rotation in ESTABLISHMENT, SPECIFIC, TAPER, RACE_WEEK or POST_EVENT weeks, nor while any exercise in use is in return steps (R6-ROTATION C6, C11).
Under COACH_DECIDES and EVERY_6_WEEKS an accessory rotates only at the first block boundary on or after its policy cadence (everyWeeks 6), never at every 4-week boundary (R6-ROTATION C5).

A MAIN changes only at a block boundary, default keep, with a recorded reason: DELIBERATE_BLOCK_TRANSITION with a stated training purpose (phase, goal specificity, equipment or technique; never variety alone), SKILL_PROGRESSION through B0-C07 with agency, EQUIPMENT_CHANGE or ATHLETE_PREFERENCE; the new MAIN fills the same slot pattern, shares a primary muscle, is skill-admissible and is established by effort; for STRENGTH-goal athletes the change is disclosed with progress shown by block or effort because lift-specific load restarts.
Under FIXED every role is REASON_ONLY; DELIBERATE_BLOCK_TRANSITION and SKILL_PROGRESSION are offered only with explicit athlete opt-in, never applied by default.
Close variation is a ranking relation only; it grants no permission and cannot exempt a MAIN from block stability.

Reason-based substitution keeps precedence over cadence but passes the clinical screen first: pain, injury, illness or a functional limitation routes CLINICAL_HUMAN_REQUIRED for the dependent scope; ambiguous reports are ASK.

confidence.rationale: Consistent with variation trials and prior SSCTR conditions; cadences remain preferences and hybrid-specific evidence is absent.

limitations: Targeted appraisal by a software reviewer, not a systematic review; no GRADE rating performed.
Sources marked ABSTRACT_ONLY support context only, never a prescriptive rule.
Validator and witness results prove specification structure, not training efficacy or safety.
Variation trials are short and mostly in young adults.

answers.answer: Within a block the current selection remains adequate; the MAIN stays.
Material facts are a reached block boundary (executed blocks), the athlete's rotation preference (DR-113, DR-134), equipment on the date and, for a MAIN change, a recorded reason.
KEEP is always valid and is the default.
A change is not necessary for adaptation; it is a preference- or purpose-driven opportunity, and a MAIN change needs a recorded reason.
An accessory swap to an admissible alternative within one demand step; a MAIN change only at a block boundary with a reason.
Keeping the configuration is the smaller option and remains available; the change happens only when preference or purpose justifies it.
The essential stimulus is preserved; protected runs are shielded by placing first exposures away from them; lift-specific progress tracking restarts and is disclosed.
SUPPORTED_WITH_LIMITS: R6-S26, N-HAUGEN, R6-S01 and R6-S48; counterevidence R6-S27.
No cadence comparison exists; hybrid athletes unstudied; protection transfer between similar exercises uncertain.
ASK or opt-in for MAIN changes under FIXED; clinical screen first for discomfort; deferral in event phases and returns.

limitations: Null for the direct question.

applicability: Nonclinical adults progressing between configurations of one pattern, offered at block boundaries with agency.

decision.rationale: Offering one step along a same-pattern ladder at a block boundary, only after the earlier configuration was progressing and with the athlete's opt-in, followed by ramped effort-guided establishment and an always-available regression, is a cautious way to let novices reach higher-skill lifts without assessing technique. Larger jumps and subpattern-changing links need explicit limits.
preserve: Familiarity gating of HIGH skill outside the ladders
Agency at every step
SKILL_MISMATCH regression

must_not: No automatic progression.
No load transfer to the new configuration.
No ladder step in deferred phases or during return steps.
conditions: A ladder step is offered, never automatic: only at a block boundary, after the earlier configuration's final exposures in the block were ADVANCE or EARNED, with explicit athlete opt-in; SKILL_MISMATCH regression along the chain is always available.
One ladder step per configuration per block boundary; no skipped chain step.

The new configuration starts with effort-guided establishment from the lightest available load (the empty bar for barbell lifts) with an ascending ramp and technique-first instruction: at most 2 sets at RIR >= 3, no load transferred, sets returning one per executed week.
Not offered in ESTABLISHMENT, SPECIFIC, TAPER, RACE_WEEK or POST_EVENT, during return steps, or under FIXED unless the athlete opts in.
Reaching a HIGH-skill configuration through a ladder makes only that configuration admissible; general skill admissibility is unchanged.

A link that changes subpattern (push-up to pike-push-up) is a variation rather than a progression of the same movement: it may fill a PUSH slot only while another PUSH slot in the same week keeps a horizontal push.
First exposures after a ladder step follow B0-C11 placement (away from the day before and the same day before the long run or quality run when days allow).

confidence.rationale: Ladders are coaching structures supported only indirectly; safety relies on opt-in, ramped establishment and regression.

limitations: Targeted appraisal by a software reviewer, not a systematic review; no GRADE rating performed.
Sources marked ABSTRACT_ONLY support context only, never a prescriptive rule.
Validator and witness results prove specification structure, not training efficacy or safety.
No direct evidence for any specific chain.

Logged final exposures with ADVANCE or EARNED gates at a block boundary; athlete opt-in.
KEEP is valid and is the default.
Not necessary for adaptation; offered for progression continuity and preference.
One ladder step with effort-guided establishment.

Novelty cost and a restart of lift-specific load tracking are traded for access to a new lift; placement protects key runs.

sources.title: The Effect of a Resistance Training Session on Physiological and Thermoregulatory Measures of Sub-maximal Running Performance in the Heat in Heat-Acclimatized Men
sources.authors: Doma K, Nicholls A, Gahreman D, Damas F, Libardi CA, Sinclair W
sources.population_design_dose: 10 resistance-untrained men; one 6RM lower-body session; submaximal running at 70% of ventilatory threshold in heat before and 24 and 48 h after.
sources.findings: Soreness increased and countermovement jump fell for 48 h; the physiological cost of submaximal running was raised for up to 48 h (ES 0.50-0.84); thermoregulation was unchanged.
sources.locator: Reused R6 source (r12 manifest); local Europe PMC XML audits/domain-coaching-r6-2026-10-26/reviews/ssctr-evidence/PMC6548784.xml, SHA-256 re-verified equal to the manifest on 2026-10-31; re-read this session: abstract and results summary.

counterevidence: Accustomed lifters show smaller effects (repeated-bout effect).

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of systematic reviews of randomized trials (>= 6 weeks) in healthy adults, mostly novices; standard, circuit, elastic-band and home-based resistance training versus control and between prescriptions.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control, including elastic-band and home-based training. Strength is enhanced by >= 2 sessions/week, heavier loads, multiple sets and exercise at the start of the session and is not affected by machines versus free weights. Hypertrophy is enhanced by >= 10 sets/muscle group/week and is not affected by frequency when volume is equated. Data are insufficient for varied exercise selection, single- versus multi-joint hypertrophy, Nordic hamstring and Olympic-style lifting. Periodization and variation are less important than once thought.
sources.locator: Reused R6 source (r12 manifest); local Europe PMC XML audits/domain-coaching-r6-2026-10-26/reviews/ssctr-evidence/PMC12965823.xml, SHA-256 re-verified equal to the manifest on 2026-10-31; re-read this session: Eligibility Criteria; Results (Strength, Hypertrophy, Improving hypertrophy); Discussion (progressive overload, specificity and individualization, variation).
limitations: Overview of reviews dominated by novice trainees; not concurrent-training or runner specific.
Exercise-level choices (which squat, row or calf raise) are not compared.
counterevidence: Insufficient data on varied selection and single- versus multi-joint hypertrophy; no specific configuration is shown superior.

sources.population_design_dose: 34 sedentary men; 8 weeks; 2 sessions/week; 7 exercises; one set versus three sets versus control.
sources.findings: Both single-set and three-set training improved strength and size; three sets gave larger gains (squat 1RM +14.8%, leg CSA +11.3%).

sources.title: The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains.
sources.authors: Pelland JC, Remmert JF, Robinson ZP, Hinson SR, Zourdos MC.
sources.population_design_dose: Bayesian multilevel meta-regressions of 67 studies (2058 participants) of weekly set volume and frequency.
sources.findings: Fractional set counting (indirect sets = 0.5) had the strongest relative evidence; volume increases hypertrophy and strength with diminishing returns; frequency increases strength (diminishing returns) with negligible effect on hypertrophy.
sources.locator: Abstract read on 2026-10-31.
limitations: Abstract only; mostly young men.
counterevidence: Dose-response curves are group means, not individual prescriptions.

sources.title: Acute Neuromuscular, Physiological and Performance Responses After Strength Training in Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: de Carvalho e Silva GI, Brandao LHA, dos Santos Silva D, de Jesus Alves MD, Aidar FJ, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Systematic review and meta-analysis (19 studies) of acute responses of recreational and trained runners to a lower-body strength session, immediately and 24-48 h later.
sources.findings: Peak torque fell and soreness, creatine kinase and perceived exertion rose; jump height, ventilation, VO2, lactate and heart rate did not differ; time to exhaustion fell in 3 of 4 studies; the authors advise limiting muscle damage before competition.

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: Searched dose-response of frequency and volume (Q13) and acute effects of strength sessions on running (Q18). Counterevidence: strength gains rise with frequency and volume with diminishing returns (Pelland 2026, abstract), so the cap may slightly slow early strength gains.

claims.statement: Strength is enhanced by >= 2 sessions per week and by higher volume, hypertrophy is unaffected by frequency when volume is equated, and most evidence is from novices.
limitations: Not hybrid-specific.
counterevidence: Higher frequency adds strength (N-PELLAND).

claims.statement: In sedentary men, both single-set and three-set programmes at two sessions per week improved strength and size over 8 weeks, three sets more.
limitations: Small sample; men only.
counterevidence: Larger volume gives larger gains.

claims.statement: Strength gains increase with frequency and volume with diminishing returns.
limitations: Abstract only.
counterevidence: Group-level model.

claims.statement: An unaccustomed strength session raises soreness and impairs subsequent running for 24-48 h, so lower early novelty matters for hybrid novices.
limitations: Harder protocols than establishment doses.
counterevidence: Accustomed lifters show smaller effects.

applicability: Strength class NONE (no current known dose, novice) from establishment until the first strength block boundary.

decision.rationale: Two full-body sessions per week give untrained adults the frequency and volume that produce early strength and size gains while limiting first-exposure novelty in a week that may also contain new running. DR-112 already requires extra days to spread rather than add load; TPL.CORE keeps every chosen day as a light session. The cost is a possibly slightly slower early strength gain, reversible at the first block boundary.
preserve: Chosen days kept (DR-112)
Establishment rules for class NONE
decision.mec_change_level: Composition cap for the first block only; no dose change per template.
decision.trade_off: Slightly lower early frequency and volume for lower novelty and better coexistence with new running.
must_not: No dropped chosen day.
No cap presented as a physiological limit or injury-prevention rule.
No catch-up of sets after release.
conditions: Applies only to strength class NONE, from establishment until the first strength block boundary; FAMILIAR_UNKNOWN_LOAD and KNOWN_LOAD classes keep the R6 day-count templates.

Release at the first block boundary requires executed evidence: the loaded configurations established (FROM_LOG adopted or KNOWN) with final exposures ADVANCE or EARNED and no repeated adverse response; otherwise the cap continues and is re-assessed at the next boundary.
On release every configuration new to the athlete starts with effort-guided establishment; sets follow R6 rules; no catch-up of sets not done.

TPL.CORE days run at practice or accessory dose with the practice configuration first, never add lower-body MAIN work, and are disclosed as lighter by design with the non-blocking STRENGTH_DAYS_ABOVE_CURRENT_PRACTICE options (keep the days lighter or choose fewer); chosen days are never dropped (DR-112).
The cap is a reversible coaching choice, not a physiological limit or injury-prevention rule.

confidence.rationale: Consistent with novice frequency and volume evidence and DR-112; the exact release point is an operational choice.

limitations: Targeted appraisal by a software reviewer, not a systematic review; no GRADE rating performed.
Sources marked ABSTRACT_ONLY support context only, never a prescriptive rule.
Validator and witness results prove specification structure, not training efficacy or safety.
No hybrid-novice trial compares two versus three or four early strength sessions.

answers.answer: The R6 day-count templates are adequate in principle but add weekly sets and new exercises for a novice before any load is established.
Strength class NONE and the chosen strength days are supplied facts; executed evidence decides release.
KEEP (R6 templates) is defensible but adds novelty and volume in the first block.
A smaller first-block load is warranted by DR-112 and conservative establishment, relative to the R6 comparator.
Cap at two full templates with TPL.CORE on further days until the first block boundary.
Keeping the R6 templates adds novelty; dropping days violates DR-112; neither is a smaller sufficient option.
Main lifts stay twice-weekly for push and pull and weekly for squat, hinge and lunge; running coexists with less soreness.
SUPPORTED_WITH_LIMITS: R6-S01 and R6-S52; counterevidence N-PELLAND.
Optimal novice frequency in hybrid weeks is unknown.
The negotiation option is disclosed (ASK-like, non-blocking); no clinical dependency.

sources.title: Effects of training with elastic resistance versus conventional resistance on muscular strength: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Lopes JSS, Machado AF, Micheletti JK, de Almeida AC, Cavina AP, Pastre CM.
sources.population_design_dose: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 trials comparing elastic resistance (tubes, bands) with conventional resistance (machines, dumbbells) for strength in varied populations.
sources.findings: No difference between elastic and conventional resistance for lower-limb (SMD -0.11, 95% CI -0.40 to 0.19) or upper-limb strength (SMD 0.09, -0.18 to 0.35) per the corrected abstract; the 2020 corrigendum (PMC7485002) fixes a reporting error (-0.011 to -0.11).
sources.locator: Read: Abstract, Introduction, Discussion and limitations; corrigendum PMC7485002 read. Retrieved full-text XML SHA-256 248b470624788bf379bb723bf254ab4f9fa5f0fb87a6368aeff781da28aef8a1.
limitations: 8 heterogeneous low-quality trials; elastic load not standardized; mixed populations including clinical.
counterevidence: Standard resistance training improved multicomponent function more than elastic training in one comparison (R6-S01).

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
sources.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, Lowisz CV, Rawson ES, Schoenfeld BJ, Smith-Ryan AE, et al.
sources.population_design_dose: Overview of systematic reviews of randomized trials (>= 6 weeks) in healthy adults, mostly novices; standard, circuit, elastic-band and home-based resistance training versus control and between prescriptions.
sources.findings: Resistance training improves strength and hypertrophy versus control, including elastic-band and home-based training. Strength is enhanced by >= 2 sessions/week, heavier loads, multiple sets and exercise at the start of the session and is not affected by machines versus free weights. Hypertrophy is enhanced by >= 10 sets/muscle group/week and is not affected by frequency when volume is equated. Data are insufficient for varied exercise selection, single- versus multi-joint hypertrophy, Nordic hamstring and Olympic-style lifting. Periodization and variation are less important than once thought.

sources.title: Effect of free-weight vs. machine-based strength training on maximal strength, hypertrophy and jump performance - a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Haugen ME, Vårvik FT, Larsen S, Haugen AS, van den Tillaar R, Bjørnsen T.
sources.population_design_dose: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 trials (1016 adults aged 18-60) directly comparing free-weight and machine-based strength training for >= 6 weeks.
sources.findings: No difference in direct comparison for dynamic strength (SMD 0.084), isometric strength, jump height or hypertrophy (SMD -0.055); strength gains are specific to the trained modality (free-weight tests favour free-weight training, SMD -0.21).
sources.locator: Read: Abstract, Methodological quality, Conclusion and Key points. Retrieved full-text XML SHA-256 dd1f66b597abdd99a8c0d88d86588ded8380a0d2b793b98fbdd8390fe805872d.
limitations: Few hypertrophy studies (n = 5); mixed training status.
counterevidence: Specificity: progress on one lift does not transfer fully to another.

literature_snapshot.counterevidence_search: Searched acute strength-to-run effects (Q18), muscle damage and running (Q10), repeated-bout evidence (Q11, Q21) and axial loading (Q22). Counterevidence: submaximal running physiology is often unchanged after strength work (R6-S53); study protocols are far more damaging than establishment doses; effects can last to 48 h, beyond the 30-h bin; no evidence on axial class (null).

claims.statement: After a lower-body strength session runners show reduced peak torque and increased soreness, creatine kinase and perceived exertion, and time to exhaustion fell in 3 of 4 studies, while submaximal physiology changed little (outcomes up to 48 h).
limitations: Small heterogeneous studies; damaging protocols.
counterevidence: Submaximal running often unaffected.

claims.statement: A 6RM lower-body session raised the physiological cost of submaximal running for up to 48 h in resistance-untrained men.
limitations: n = 10; heat; heavy session.
counterevidence: Accustomed lifters respond less.

claims.statement: The first bout of unaccustomed eccentric work causes more damage than a repeated bout, with protection lasting up to 6-9 weeks.
limitations: Maximal eccentric protocol in young men.
counterevidence: Training at 2-3 RIR damages far less.

claims.statement: Across 20 studies of multi-joint exercises the first bout produced more soreness, creatine kinase, strength and jump loss and higher VO2 and RPE in running-economy tests at 24-48 h than the second.
limitations: Abstract only.
counterevidence: None.

claims.statement: Damaging plyometric work reduced a 30-min running time trial by 4% at 48 h in moderately trained runners.
limitations: Abstract only; deliberately damaging protocol.
counterevidence: None.

claims.statement: No study links axial (spinal) loading class to subsequent running performance, so the axial tie-break is an implementation choice, not evidence.
limitations: Null search Q22.
counterevidence: Axial-HIGH lifts are also the heaviest systemic lifts (plausible proxy).

applicability: Placement and ranking of lower-body strength relative to the long run and the week's quality run within chosen days and shifts (DR-112); ordinal costs only.

decision.rationale: Unaccustomed and eccentric-dominant lower-body work impairs subsequent harder or prolonged running for about a day or more and is attenuated by a repeated bout, so a separate ordinal novelty and eccentric cost before protected runs is a distinct construct from the existing lower-demand bins and implements SIS section 5 and the OB-2 conditions. It must stay a ranking signal, avoid double counting, never introduce new or HIGH-eccentric work as a substitute, respect the phase lead and treat the axial tie-break as an implementation choice.
preserve: Ordinal costs; Pareto then leximax ranking
Chosen days and shifts as hard constraints (DR-112)
No hour rule (POL-07)
decision.mec_change_level: Ranking cost and placement preference; content changes only after arrangement options fail.
decision.trade_off: Protects the long run and quality run under RUN lead; under STRENGTH lead the long run's content may yield instead.
must_not: No prohibition derived from the 30-h bin.
No first-exposure or HIGH-eccentric substitute the day before a protected run.
No reduced lower-body dose presented as recovery or injury prevention.
conditions: CMP.I11 is an ordinal ranking cost: LOW, counted once per pair of strength session and protected run whatever the number of qualifying rows, never a prohibition or hour rule (POL-07; R6-HYBRID-ARRANGEMENT C10); athlete evidence may raise it for that athlete only.
It applies before RUN.LONG and the week's protected quality KEY run (threshold, event-specific or B0-C02 familiar bouts); race proximity stays under CMP.I01 and CMP.P06.
Arrangement first: within the chosen days and shifts (DR-112) prefer placements and orders that avoid the cost; content changes only when none exists.

Content reduction (CMP.P04, CMP.P05 and PROTECTED_RUN_STIMULUS_CONFLICT) uses only an established or familiar non-HIGH-eccentric configuration of the same pattern, or fewer sets of the current configuration under the R6 dose adjustment; it never introduces a first-exposure or HIGH-eccentric configuration on the day before or the same day before the protected run.

Under STRENGTH lead the long run's content may yield instead and a MAIN is not replaced for a run-protection reason; under JOINT a genuine equal-harm trade-off is asked once; under RUN lead strength keeps its essential stimulus (main lifts at goal or phase dose).
The axial tie-break is an IMPLEMENTATION_CHOICE (plausible, not evidence-based): it only decides which of otherwise equal rows is reduced or replaced first and never creates a cost or score.
Every kept MODERATE-or-higher cost and every content reduction is disclosed with its trade-off; a reduced lower-body dose is never presented as a recovery or injury-prevention measure.
PROTECTED_RUN_STIMULUS_CONFLICT is governed by this record, not by R6-HYBRID-ARRANGEMENT.

confidence.rationale: Acute and repeated-bout evidence is consistent in direction; magnitudes at establishment doses are unknown and the axial dimension is unsupported.

limitations: Targeted appraisal by a software reviewer, not a systematic review; no GRADE rating performed.
Sources marked ABSTRACT_ONLY support context only, never a prescriptive rule.
Validator and witness results prove specification structure, not training efficacy or safety.
Effects can persist to 48 h; the 30-h bin is a ranking convention, not a recovery time.

answers.answer: An arrangement with HIGH-eccentric or new lower-body work the day before, or the same day before, the long run or quality run may impair the protected run.
Session contents (eccentric class, first or re-establishment exposure from the ledger), chosen days and shifts, the protected run and the phase lead are supplied facts.
KEEP is defensible when no alternative arrangement exists, with disclosure.
Relative to the R6 costs, which ignore novelty and eccentric demand, a ranking signal is warranted; content change is necessary only when arrangement options fail.
Arrangement first, then an established non-HIGH-eccentric same-pattern configuration or fewer sets, then the long run's content under STRENGTH lead.
A ranking cost is the smallest tool; replacing exercises is reserved for cases where arrangement cannot protect the run.
Protects the run-led stimulus while strength keeps its essential stimulus; under STRENGTH lead the strength session is protected.
SUPPORTED_WITH_LIMITS: R6-S53, R6-S09 and R6-S48 (full text), N-DOMA23 and N-MARCORA (abstracts); axial unsupported.
Dose-response at establishment doses; residual effects between 30 and 48 h; individual variation.
ASK on a genuine JOINT trade-off; clinical routing unchanged; no HOLD needed.

sources.title: Compatibility of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Training for Skeletal Muscle Size and Function: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.authors: Schumann M, Feuerbacher JF, Sunkeler M, Freitag N, Ronnestad BR, Doma K, Lundberg TR

limitations: Heterogeneous protocols; mostly untrained or recreationally active participants; chronic outcomes only.
counterevidence: Interference depends on modality, frequency and order; it is not established for any particular day layout.

sources.authors: Eddens L, van Someren K, Howatson G

counterevidence: Single small trials have favoured the opposite order for jumps and VO2max.
